An 8-year-old, previously healthy, fully immunized girl presented with 5 days of intermittent fever followed by abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had been at home due to the COVID-19 pandemic; her parents had mild upper respiratory symptoms for 1 week. Outpatient oral antibiotics and IV fluids did not improve her symptoms. She was admitted to surgery with suspected appendicitis; abdominal ultrasonography was normal. Persistent fever, abdominal pain, and the emergence of a rash and conjunctivitis prompted transfer to the pediatric COVID-19 ward. 

On examination, temperature was 38.6 °C. She had bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, erythematous throat, palmar erythema, a strawberry tongue, and an erythema multiforme–type rash; there was no hypotension, lymphadenopathy, or respiratory distress. Cardiac examination revealed a grade II/VI murmur at the left sternal border; lung sounds were normal.

Laboratory tests showed ESR 67 mm/h, CRP 166 mg/L, platelet count 192×10^9/L, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and WBC 10.3×10^9/L with 82% neutrophils. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Urinalysis and urine culture were negative. A high-resolution chest CT scan was not indicative of COVID-19. Reverse transcription PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and blood cultures were negative.

A 50-year-old Indian woman with diabetes and hypertension presented with right upper abdominal discomfort, loss of appetite, and low-grade fever. She denied jaundice.  
On examination, she had hepatomegaly and tenderness in the right hypochondrium.  
Laboratory studies showed normal liver-function tests. Serological tests for amoebiasis and hydatid disease were negative. A chest radiograph was normal.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an 11 × 7.5 × 11.2 cm predominantly anechoic, thick-walled lesion arising from the inferior surface of the liver, with low-level internal echoes and a homogeneous echogenic area in its superolateral portion. The gallbladder was not visualized separately; other abdominal viscera were normal.  
Aspiration of the lesion yielded turbid fluid, but the lesion persisted despite repeated aspirations and antibiotic therapy.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, lobulated cystic lesion with a solid component in its superior part, abutting the colon and duodenum. The lesion was interpreted as an infected non-parasitic cyst.

A 74-year-old right-handed woman was brought to the psychiatry clinic with a 5-month history of abrupt onset of disorganized speech, severe anxiety, and self-harm behaviors that began after a family trip. Her speech was rapid, fluent, and nonsensical—exemplified by the phrase “Our neighbor has gone to the cobbler to buy Ghormeh Sabzi”—consistent with Wernicke’s aphasia. Over the ensuing months, she developed agitation, persecutory delusions, visual and auditory hallucinations, urinary and fecal incontinence, and a persistent urge to flee her home.

Her psychiatric history included a 10-year history of depression treated with sertraline. There was no prior cognitive impairment or neurological disease. On examination, she was disoriented to time, demonstrated anomia, and had marked perseveration on the Clock Drawing Test, impaired performance on Luria’s three-step test, and defective crossed-pentagon drawing. Cognitive testing revealed an MMSE score of 2/30 and an ACE-R score of 2/100, likely confounded by comprehension deficits.

An initial brain MRI performed 2 months after symptom onset was reported as normal. She was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and started on memantine and quetiapine, without clinical improvement. Because of the acute presentation and prominent frontal and temporal features, she was referred to neurology for further assessment.

A 59-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus presented with one day of left-sided weakness, left facial paresis, difficulty speaking, and drowsiness. His NIH Stroke Scale score on admission was 10. He denied recent head trauma or family history of stroke or thrombosis. He was a non-smoker but used opiates.  

On examination, he was confused and could not follow commands. Temperature was 37.4 °C, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg, heart rate 73 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There was no pallor, jaundice, petechiae, or organomegaly. Cranial-nerve exam was normal except for left facial paresis. Motor testing showed left hemiparesis (3/5 in the arm, 4/5 in the leg) with decreased pain response on the left and an upgoing plantar response on that side.  

An ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. A noncontrast head CT performed >24 h after symptom onset revealed an acute right MCA territory infarct in the right parietotemporal lobe. Twenty-four hours later, because of worsening consciousness, a repeat CT showed a new infarct in the left frontal lobe (left MCA territory).  

Initial laboratory results included a platelet count of 77 × 10^3/μL and hemoglobin 15 g/dL. Over the next several days, the platelet count declined to 21 × 10^3/μL, and hemoglobin fell to 11.8 g/dL. An 87-year-old Cantonese-speaking man with Alzheimer’s dementia, hypertension, stroke, hyperlipidaemia, gout, peptic ulcer, and chronic kidney disease presented with one week of increasing left leg pain and weakness, impaired mobility, and a single episode of urinary incontinence. He also reported anorexia and a 12% body-weight loss over six months.  
On examination, his blood pressure was 88/45 mmHg (responsive to IV fluids), heart rate 96/min, temperature 36.4 °C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He weighed 51 kg (BMI 19 kg/m2). Cardiac and chest examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination was normal. Neurologic examination showed 4/5 strength in left hip and knee flexors and extensors; the rest of the exam was normal.  
Initial laboratory results demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 76 mg/L, WCC 11.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.5 × 10^9/L) and pre-renal acute-on-chronic kidney injury.  
An initial differential of cauda equina syndrome or epidural abscess prompted an urgent MRI of the lumbar spine, which showed mild foraminal narrowing at L5–S1 but no central canal stenosis or abscess. He was admitted for possible sepsis; chest X-ray, atypical pneumonia serology, and urine microscopy and culture were all unremarkable. A plain X-ray of the left hip showed no fracture.  
Despite analgesia, his left hip pain worsened, strength declined to 2/5 at the hip and 3/5 at the knee, and CRP and ESR continued to rise. A left hip ultrasound revealed a small anterior joint effusion. Normal tumour markers, MRI of the hip, and an isotope bone scan argued against malignancy. Attempts at hip aspiration were unsuccessful. Colchicine was started for presumed crystal arthropathy and atorvastatin was discontinued for possible myopathy, but creatine kinase was normal, and symptoms persisted.  
An MRI of the hips and pelvis then demonstrated bilateral iliacus and iliopsoas muscle oedema with enhancement and a left-sided insertional tendinopathy, with no evidence of trochanteric bursitis.

MRI confirmed a large right retroperitoneal predominantly fatty mass in the location of the right adrenal gland measuring 15.6 × 11.7 × 10.4 cm, extra-renal in location, with soft-tissue nodular and linear strand-like areas showing mild enhancement on post-contrast images and no definite infiltration of adjacent organs.
